content: Zygomycota, also known as zygote fungi, represent a phylum of fungi. The name Zygomycota is derived from the term zygosporangia, which refers to the resistant, spherical spores that are formed during their sexual reproduction. Approximately 600 species of zygomycetes have been identified. These fungi are predominantly terrestrial, inhabiting soil or decomposing organic matter such as decaying plants or animal material. The hyphae of zygomycetes are often coenocytic, meaning they lack septa, except in specific cases such as during gamete formation or when isolating dead hyphal segments. A well-known example of a zygomycete is Rhizopus stolonifer, a member of the order Mucorales. This fungus is commonly observed growing on bread and other food items. It spreads across the surface of its substrate and extends hyphae inward to absorb nutrients. During its asexual reproductive phase, it produces bulbous black sporangia at the tips of upright hyphae. Each sporangium contains hundreds of haploid spores. When mycelia of complementary mating types are present, the fungus undergoes sexual reproduction, resulting in the formation of zygosporangia. These zygosporangia are characterized by their thick walls, which make them highly resistant to adverse environmental conditions. They remain metabolically inactive until environmental conditions improve, at which point they germinate to produce either a sporangium or vegetative hyphae. Certain zygomycetes have evolved specialized mechanisms for spore dispersal. For instance, Pilobolus, a fungus that grows on animal dung, uses a light-sensitive pigment to orient its sporangiophores toward light. This mechanism allows the sporangia to be launched up to 2 meters away, increasing the likelihood of landing on vegetation that may be consumed by herbivores. The spores are subsequently deposited in new locations along with the animal's dung. Other members of the zygomycete order Entomophthorales have also developed unique methods for forcibly discharging their spores. From a phylogenetic perspective, Zygomycota are considered to occupy a basal position in the fungal evolutionary tree, having diverged from other fungi after the chytrids. Molecular phylogenetic studies have revealed that Zygomycota form a polyphyletic group, suggesting that they may eventually be divided into several distinct phyla. Notably, the order Glomales was reclassified in 2001 and elevated to the division Glomeromycota. This reclassification was based on their lack of zygospore formation, their mycorrhizal associations, and the absence of DNA sequence homology with other zygomycetes.
